property_summary: After initializing c, SetMinSum must still allow updating MinSum (i.e. MinSum can be changed after Initialized() is called).
SetMinSum must succeed (not revert) when called before Initialized() has been called and must revert when called after Initialized() has been called.
Once c.Initialized() has been called, SetMinSum cannot change MinSum (it remains equal to the value set earlier).

If MinSum is set via SetMinSum then subsequent calls to Put from that setter cannot result in the setter's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance being zero (i.e., setting MinSum does not allow its setter to make a zero-value deposit afterwards).
SetMinSum may be called with any uint value (including zero) before initialization; the original contract never reverts on that precondition, while the mutant rejects zero.

For any caller and any uint _val, if SetMinSum(_val) returns normally then MinSum equals _val (the reference only updates MinSum when not initialized), whereas the mutant can write MinSum before the initialization guard and thus can make MinSum equal _val even when the call should have reverted or later interactions differ.

For any caller and any value, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the reference either leaves MinSum unchanged when the contract is already initialized (call reverts) or sets MinSum to _val when not initialized; the mutant can set MinSum even when initialized by assigning before the revert, so there exists an input where MinSum differs after a call.

For every caller and value, if the contract has been initialized then calling SetMinSum(...) must leave MinSum unchanged (the call reverts); the mutant that assigns before the initialized check can change MinSum despite initialization for some fuzzed _val and thus violates this invariant.

For every uint _val and caller, if the contract has been Initialized() then SetMinSum(_val) must not change MinSum (call reverts and MinSum stays as before); the mutant that assigns before the initialized guard can cause MinSum to change for some fuzzed _val and thus violate this invariant.

For any caller and any uint newVal, if the caller calls SetLogFile(...) with an address whose AddMessage will revert (a reverter helper), then afterward calling SetMinSum(newVal) must either (a) revert leaving MinSum unchanged when Initialized() was already called, or (b) set MinSum to newVal only when not initialized; the mutant that writes MinSum before the initialized check can leave MinSum equal to newVal even when the call would later revert under an adversarial external log callee — so there exists a fuzzed newVal and adversarial log address where the mutant's MinSum differs from the reference.
SetMinSum cannot succeed once Initialized() has been called (i.e., Initialized() makes future SetMinSum revert).
SetMinSum only succeeds when intitalized is false (i.e., it reverts if initialized is true).

Calling SetMinSum(x) on the correct contract always sets MinSum exactly to x on the first non-initialized call (overwrites previous value), whereas the mutant accumulates (MinSum increases by x), so for some fuzzed x and sequence of two calls the final MinSum differs between reference and mutant.

For every uint _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the reference sets MinSum equal to _val (no sign change); the mutant negates _val before assignment, so there exist inputs where MinSum != _val and thus differs from the reference.

For any uint input _val, after calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract C, the public MinSum equals the provided _val; the mutant that writes 0 instead breaks this by making MinSum == 0 for some nonzero _val inputs.

SetLogFile can only succeed (no revert) before Initialized() is called, so calling SetLogFile before Initialized leaves address(c).balance unchanged and does not revert when intitalized is false in original but would revert in mutant.
Calling SetLogFile should succeed (not revert) whenever the contract has not yet been Initialized.
Once Initialized() has been called, SetLogFile must revert (not change Log); the mutant breaks this by allowing SetLogFile to overwrite Log after initialization.

Calling SetLogFile(address) on the correct contract sets the Log storage slot (the LogFile-typed variable) via its public getter remaining nonzero when given a nonzero address whereas the mutant writes the address into MinSum instead so for some addresses the Log getter will remain zero while MinSum changes; thus for all addresses 0 the behavior is consistent but for some nonzero addresses the reference makes Log nonzero while the mutant does not.

For every nonzero address passed to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that address in the Log public variable (so address(c.Log()) == provided address) while the mutant writes the value into MinSum instead, making address(c.Log()) differ for some nonzero addresses; the test fuzzes an address and asserts that after SetLogFile the Log getter equals the provided address.

For every non-zero address input, calling SetLogFile on the correct contract stores that address in the Log public variable (so address(c.Log()) == addr), while the mutant instead writes the address into MinSum and leaves Log unchanged for some non-zero addresses, so there exists an address input where address(c.Log()) != addr.

For every address input x, calling SetLogFile(x) on the correct contract stores x into the Log public variable (so address(c.Log()) equals x) whereas the mutant writes the numeric value into MinSum instead, so there exist addresses x for which address(c.Log()) != x (the mutant breaks this rule).

For every non-zero address A, calling SetLogFile(A) on the correct contract stores A into the public Log variable (so address(c.Log()) == A); the mutant instead writes the numeric value into MinSum and does not set Log, so there exist non-zero addresses where address(c.Log()) != A.

For any caller address and any log-address argument, calling SetLogFile on the correct contract never reverts when intitalized is false and always sets the Log pointer to the provided address; the mutant reverts after assignment only when intitalized is true causing a difference in whether the call completes and whether Log is updated for some inputs (specifically when intitalized is true).

For any address arg, calling SetLogFile(x) on a fresh contract either (A) when intitalized is false always returns success and sets Log to x, or (B) when intitalized is true the reference will revert (so call fails) without having changed Log previously; the mutant assigns Log before checking intitalized, so there exist inputs (call sequence with Initialized() called before SetLogFile) where the mutant still reverts but leaves Log set while the reference would never have set Log in that scenario — we assert that when the contract is initialized, attempts to call SetLogFile must not change the stored Log pointer (i.e. the call either succeeds and sets Log or it reverts and leaves Log unchanged), a rule the reference preserves but the mutant violates.

After initialization, any call to SetLogFile must not leave Log changed when the call reverts; the mutant assigns Log before reverting when initialized, so there exist inputs (call sequence where Initialized() was called and then SetLogFile is invoked) where the mutant leaves Log updated despite the call reverting, violating the rule.

For all inputs, calling SetLogFile either succeeds and sets the Log pointer to the supplied address, or (if it reverts because the contract was already initialized) it must leave the stored Log pointer unchanged; the mutant assigns Log before checking initialized, so when initialized it can revert while still changing Log.

If SetLogFile reverts (call does not complete) then the public Log pointer must remain equal to its pre-call value; the mutant assigns Log before reverting when initialized, so for some inputs a reverted SetLogFile still changes Log.

For any nonzero address input, calling SetLogFile(x) on the correct contract stores Log != address(0) (i.e., the stored Log getter returns the provided nonzero address), whereas the mutant overwrites the input and sets Log to address(0) for some inputs, so there exists an address input for which the reference preserves a nonzero Log but the mutant leaves it zero.

For any nonzero address supplied to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that address (Log getter != address(0)), whereas the mutant overwrites the input with address(0) causing Log to become address(0) for some nonzero inputs; we assert that after calling SetLogFile with any address param, the stored Log address equals the provided address (i.e., not zero when input nonzero).

For any address parameter passed to SetLogFile on the correct contract, after the call the public Log getter returns that same address (i.e. the stored Log equals the provided address); the mutant overwrites the input with address(0) so for some inputs the stored Log becomes address(0) and thus differs from the provided address.

For every nonzero address input, calling SetLogFile(addr) on the correct contract results in the public Log getter returning that same address (i.e. Log != address(0)), whereas the mutant overwrites the input with address(0) so there exist inputs for which the stored Log becomes address(0) and thus differs from the provided address.

For every address input x, calling SetLogFile(x) on the correct contract results in the stored Log getter returning x (i.e. Log() == x), but the mutant overwrites the input with address(0) making Log() == address(0) for some x — so the property is: after SetLogFile(x), c.Log() == x.
After depositing with a lock, the stored unlockTime for the caller is always an absolute timestamp greater than or equal to block.timestamp.

If a Put call with lock duration L reverts then L is less than the current stored unlock duration for the caller (i.e. new absolute unlock would not extend existing one), so Put should only revert when L <= previous relative unlock value.
Calling Put on the original contract never reverts, so the test requires that calling c.Put(_lockTime) succeeds (reverted == false).
